The market sundial moved one minute. Its guardian was a dancer who never got to stop dancing.
A red kite drops out of the windless sky. Its string trails down to nobody.
A kite that never comes down. Somebody's kid flew that. Somebody's kid never got to reel it in.
The garden sundial moved one minute. Its guardian was a kite that never came down.
High in the tower, the bell that should have rung one o'clock swings back — and comes for you.
Bells should not be permitted to fight. It's unchivalrous.
Bram, you were hit by a bell.
Exactly my point.
The bell-tower sundial moved one minute. Its guardian was the bell that should have rung one o'clock.
A fisherman, mid-cast. The plaque reads: TO BE RETURNED.
A Dawnguard knight with a kind, tired face. The plaque reads: SIR ALDOUS VENN — TO BE RETURNED.
A blind woman with her eyes closed, smiling at something no one else can see. TAMSIN OF SALTGLASS — TO BE RETURNED. Someone has scratched underneath, very small: SHE WOULD NOT HAVE WANTED THIS.
She wouldn't have. She'd have smacked him with her stick.
A man in a fisherman's cap, with Wren's chin and Wren's crooked smile. EDRIN HALLOWAY — TO BE RETURNED.
It's a good likeness. He always looked like he was about to say something funny.
A woman in a Keeper's robes, braid over one shoulder. The marble is new; the dust has not settled on it yet. YSOLDE HALLOWAY — TO BE RETURNED.
He made her a statue. He made her a STATUE.
Wren—
I'm fine. I'm — let's ring the bell.
A girl of ten, mid-laugh, ribbon flying. The plaque has been carved and re-carved so many times the letters are deep as wounds. It says only: FIRST.
He made her laughing. Of course he did.
Letters. Thousands of them, from every corner of Solmere, every one answered and filed. "Dear Hierophant, my son is sick." "Dear Hierophant, the Lantern in our village has gone dim."

A shelf labeled HALLOWAY, W. Every letter you ever wrote him, pressed flat. Beside each, a note in his hand: "Restless. Like L." "Asks where the sun goes. Like L." "Wants to leave the island. Like L."
He wasn't writing to me. He was writing to her.
He was writing to both of you. That's worse.
A shelf labeled VESPERSONG — DRAFTS. Forty years of music. The earliest pages are in a boy's handwriting, with the notes drawn as little suns.

An unfinished letter on the desk: "Dear Wren — By the time you read this, the sun will have stopped, and you will never have to lose anyone again. I'm sorry it had to be your mother's Dawnstone. I'm sorry for—" Nothing more. The ink has dried on the nib.
Didn't finish the sorry. Man never could.
Three things: eat something, sleep a little, and don't die tomorrow. Physician's orders.
Three things.
Of course.
One. When we were six, you told me you'd leave the island one day, and I'd stay and be a boring herbalist, and you'd send me postcards. I cried for a week.
I didn't know that.
You weren't supposed to. Two. When you gave him the Dawnstone, I wanted you to hurt as much as everyone else did. For a whole year I wanted that.
Three. I stopped. Not because you deserved it. Because I deserved to put it down. It was heavy, Wren. I carried it everywhere. I couldn't hold anything else.
What do you want to hold instead?
A hospital. A real one, with windows. A day off. And I want to be bad at something, on purpose. Painting. Or the fiddle.
You'd be terrible at the fiddle.
I know. Isn't it wonderful?
The light said Mender and I said yes, because it was expected. Now I'd say yes anyway. That's the difference. That's the whole difference.
If I freeze tomorrow, kick me. Gently. Then less gently.
Wren. May I confess something? It's not dignified.
When has that ever stopped you?
Fair. I'm scared. Not ordinary scared — bone-scared. The kind I had at my knighting trial, when I froze, and Sir Aldous...
I always thought the brave ones didn't feel it. I thought there was a sort of valve. A spiritual cork. And I was born without one.
Then I met him. Down there. Seventeen and shaking like a wet dog, and holding his spear anyway.
